The question of when the Word of Wisdom became mandatory is contested across sources, with different dates cited depending on what "mandatory" means. According to d5 (Dialogue Journal) and d7 (Church of Jesus Christ official manual), on September 9, 1851, President Brigham Young proposed that all Saints formally covenant to keep the Word of Wisdom, and the motion was "accepted unanimously and became binding as a commandment for all Church members thereafter" [d7]. However, d8 (Church History Library, an official LDS source) states that "in 1919, the First Presidency under President Heber J. Grant made observing the Word of Wisdom a requirement for receiving a temple recommend," suggesting the 1851 vote did not fully enforce compliance [d8]. This is corroborated by d4 (a BYU scholarly thesis), which notes that none of Grant's predecessors "required rigid compliance for procurement of a Temple recommend" and that it was under Grant's administration that "strict observance became a criterion of orthodoxy" [d4]. Sources further diverge on the precise year of the temple recommend requirement: d6 gives 1921, d2 gives 1915, and d9 cites an October 8, 1919 First Presidency letter [d6][d2][d9]. In sum, while 1851 is widely cited as when it was declared a commandment by covenant, the stricter enforcement as a temple worthiness requirement came in the 1919–1921 period under Heber J. Grant, with sources disagreeing on the exact year.
